title: Wavefront backpressure and fusion timestep labnotes
body:
Summary:

This note collects exploratory profiling and experiment results for a recurring latency pattern we've been seeing on longer sequences: intermittent 10–30 ms p95 spikes that correlate with certain kernel fusion configurations. The working name for the phenomenon is 'wavefront backpressure' — i.e., a ripple of scheduling/queueing pressure across attention timesteps and fused ops that amplifies small scheduling jitter into visible tail latency.

Goals:
- Reproduce spike reliably across kernels (FlashAttention vX, paged-attn, fused matmul+softmax kernels).
- Attribute spikes to scheduler/backpressure vs memory copy vs kernel code path.
- Find mitigation levers (batch shaping, fusion toggles, prefetch heuristics, scheduler parameters).
- Produce actionable experiment matrix and next steps for runtime changes.

Background / why this matters:
We have consistent customer feedback about tail-latency stutters at sequence lengths >2048 under mixed workloads. Throughput and p50 are fine; p95/p99 suffers unpredictably which breaks strict SLOs. Past notes touched on prefetch and KV cache contention; this document focuses on the interplay between fused attention kernels and request-level wavefronting (time-step aligned work arriving at the attention hotpath).

Testbed and harness:
- Hardware: 2x NVIDIA A100 80GB (driver 535.86, CUDA 12.1), single-GPU microbench runs.
- Runtime: in-tree serving-runtime dev build (branch: wavefront-experiments), pytorch 2.1.0, triton 2.1.0, compiled FlashAttention (fork) with debug timers enabled.
- Baseline kernels: flashattn-1.0 (reference), fusion-v2 (in-tree), paged-attn (experimental paged KV cache).
- Workload generator: synthetic chat workload that issues variable sequence increments (chunked 32-token generation steps) to stress timesteps; mix of short (64) and long (3072) requests.
- Measurement: per-token kernel timing traces (instrumented), NVTX spans in server, Nsight Systems capture for slow runs, and lightweight pprof-style sampling for CPU scheduling.
- Repro command (local): 
  ./tools/run_local_bench --model galactica-8b --seq 3072 --batch 4 --step-size 32 --fusion=on --flash=on --paged-kv=off --trace=timers

Observed behaviors:
1) Deterministic p95 spikes when fusion-v2 is enabled and workloads contain staggered timestep arrivals (i.e., requests that are offset by a few tokens). Spikes occur ~every 200–400ms in steady-state.
2) FlashAttention kernel invocation times individually look stable in isolation (~0.6 ms per head) but overall request tail grows because of cumulative queueing at the input-stage to the fused kernel.
3) When paged-kv is enabled, we observe additional microspikes triggered by device->host page-resolve activity (L2 misses followed by memcpy stalls). These adds irregular ~3–6 ms jitter but are distinguishable from the fusion ripple in trace alignment.

Key traces / example:
- Nsight capture (slow interval): shows repeated pattern where small CPU-side batching decisions defer a fused attention launch by ~400–800 us; subsequent launches then serialize on a single stream causing temporal bunching. The bunching increases SM occupancy transiently and evicts small transient memory (scratchpad) leading to a soft-failure path in the fused kernel where it falls back to a slower memory layout.
- Instrumented kernel timers: timeline shows steady per-kernel time but variable inter-kernel gaps; the variance of the inter-kernel gap correlates strongly with p95.

Hypotheses (short list):
A) Scheduling ripple: The runtime coalescer/scheduler groups small inflight timestep work into fused kernels. Small timing differences in arrival create variable-sized wavefronts; when these exceed fused kernel capacity we see fallback codepaths or increased synchronization waits.
B) Transient memory pressure: Bunched launches temporarily increase shared memory/register pressure that causes kernel to use a slower path (e.g., spilling or different tiling), increasing tail.
C) Stream contention: we are using single-stream serialized launches for fused kernels; alternating async/cross-stream launches might reduce serialization.
D) Paged-KV interactions: page fault or L2 miss chains can amplify any scheduler jitter into longer stalls — distinct signal but often overlapping in time.

Experiment matrix and results summary:
- Variables: fusion (on/off), flash (on/off), paged-kv (on/off), batch shape (batch batch_size per request), arrival jitter (none / 50–250us / 1–3ms), scheduler throttle (coalescer window 0–5 ms), stream strategy (single / per-request / per-layer async).
- Key runs (representative):
  * baseline (fusion off, flash on): p50 42 ms, p95 58 ms, spikes rare.
  * fusion on, single-stream, no jitter: p50 40 ms, p95 75 ms, recurrent spikes every 300 ms.
  * fusion on, per-request streams: p50 41 ms, p95 50 ms, spikes reduced dramatically.
  * fusion on + paged-kv on: p50 44 ms, p95 92 ms, distinct microspikes aligned with page resolve.
  * fusion off + paged-kv on: p50 45 ms, p95 60 ms — page-induced jitter still present but fusion amplification missing.
  * fusion-v2 with coalescer window = 0.5 ms: p95 improved ~15% vs default 2 ms.

Interpretation:
- Fusion by itself increases average latency slightly but is usually beneficial for throughput; however, under staggered arrival patterns it can amplify jitter into pronounced tail effects.
- Switching to per-request or per-layer streams (breaking the single-stream serialization) reduces the ripple because kernels can overlap instead of piling up sequentially.
- Reducing coalescer window (less aggressive batching) reduces p95 at cost of some throughput — tradeoff likely acceptable for strict SLO classes.
- Paged-KV introduces an orthogonal jitter source; avoid enabling paged-kv on hosts with high L2 miss rates or when strict tail bounds are needed.

Actionable mitigations tried (and outcomes):
1) Conservative fuse fallback: add a heuristic to disable fusion when arrival jitter > threshold. Outcome: p95 stabilizes but throughput takes ~6% hit.
2) Stream partitioning: launch per-request CUDA streams for fused kernels, fallback to serialization only when memory footprint would exceed available scratchpad. Outcome: p95 down ~20% with small CPU overhead (stream management).
3) Coalescer tuning: reduce batching window to 0.5 ms for low-latency tiers, keep 2 ms default for high-throughput tiers. Outcome: useful trade-off; need APIs for tier config.
4) Paged-KV mitigation: pre-touch pages for long requests and prefer LRU-friendly eviction patterns. Outcome: reduces paged-induced microspikes but cannot remove scheduler ripple.

Instrumentation notes / artifacts to keep: (these are links or local capture names)
- nsight/wavefront-run-2024-11-15.qdrep (captures of worst-case)
- traces/trace-wavefront-20241115.json (per-token instrumented trace)
- flamegraphs/stream-serial-vs-parallel.svg (visual)
- perf-summaries/wavefront-summary-2024-11-16.txt

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Can kernel authors make the fused path more tolerant of transient register/shared-memory pressure (so spills don't trigger huge slowdown)? Need microbench with small forced register pressure to study code paths.
- Is there an opportunity for a smarter scheduler that watches inter-arrival times and chooses fusion vs per-request streams adaptively per-request? This would remove manual tiering.
- Measure across more GPU topologies (H100, L40) to validate whether behavior is general or A100-specific.
- Evaluate interaction with other runtime features (dynamic quantization, continuous batching across multiple models).

Immediate next steps (owner assignments):
- Riya: instrument fused kernels to emit a fast path / slow path flag in timers. (JIRA: JIRA-INV-4821)
- Ben: prototype per-request stream manager and run a perf matrix on 3 GPUs. (PR: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/876)
- Miguel: extend synthetic harness to generate controlled arrival jitter patterns and produce p95 heatmaps across coalescer window sizes.
- Ayesha: write up proposed runtime config knobs (coalescer window, stream mode, fusion-bypass-until-stable-arrival) and propose default profiles for low-latency vs high-throughput tenants.

Notes to self and rough ideas:
- "Wavefront" seems useful as a mental model — consider making a short explainer slide for ops and solutions.
- Consider an in-flight metric: 'fusion-queue-depth' sampled at kernel entrance to detect buildup before it affects p95; good candidate for Console alerting.

Appendix: quick reproduction flags and envs
- ENV vars used: EXPORT RUNTIME_COALESCE_MS=2; RUNTIME_STREAM_MODE=single; RUNTIME_FUSION=1; PAGED_KV=0
- perf command used: /usr/bin/time -v ./tools/run_local_bench --model gall-8b --seq 3072 --batch 4 --step-size 32 --trace=timers
- Note: enable NVTX and Nsight capture for worst-case runs.

If anything in the runs is unclear I can attach the raw traces (nsight dumps are large) or re-run on smaller subset. This doc will be updated with microbench data and the flamegraphs once Ben's PR lands and Riya's kernel flagging is in place.

-- Ayesha
